strengths: Introduces MultiSPA, a large-scale multi-frame spatial dataset/benchmark with 27M+ QA samples from 1.1M images and 26 subtasks, covering depth, correspondence, camera motion, object motion, and object size with multiple answer formats.

The data generation pipeline is technically described and includes non-trivial components: visible-point projection, overlap-based image-pair sampling, rigid-body segmentation for dynamic points, and BFS-based coverage-set search.
The paper provides a benchmark with task-specific metrics and held-out evaluation splits, and includes code listings/templates, which improves reproducibility over purely conceptual dataset papers.

The model is trained with LoRA on InternVL2-8B and shows large gains on the proposed benchmark, with scalability trends as data/model size increases and evidence of multi-task synergy on selected tasks.

Zero-shot BLINK results are a positive external signal: Multi-SpatialMLLM improves over InternVL baselines and several proprietary models on selected multi-view/spatial splits, suggesting the learned skills transfer somewhat.
The paper reports standard VQA benchmark results to check for catastrophic forgetting, and includes a qualitative robotics demonstration, which broadens the potential application scope.
The limitations section acknowledges two-view constraints and the preliminary nature of the emergent-capability claim, showing some awareness of scope.
weaknesses: The core evaluation on MultiSPA is fundamentally in-domain: Multi-SpatialMLLM is trained on 3M QA samples from the same data-generation pipeline and templates as the benchmark, while baselines and proprietary models are not trained on this data. Large MultiSPA gains therefore mainly demonstrate task adaptation, not general multi-frame spatial understanding.

No comparison is provided against the closest spatial-reasoning MLLM baselines (e.g., SpatialVLM, SpatialRGPT, SAT) on the proposed benchmark or BLINK. This is a material omission given the paper's claim of advancing multi-frame spatial understanding.

The claimed 'multi-frame' contribution is narrower than advertised: several tasks are single-image (depth estimation/value), object-size tasks use only image pairs and ground-truth 3D bounding-box dimensions, and the appendix admits most experiments use only two-view scenarios.

Object-size QA may be solvable largely from object-category priors rather than multi-view spatial reasoning: answers are taken from 3D bounding boxes of commonly seen objects, so the model need not necessarily integrate multiple images to infer size.

The 'emergent capability' claim is overinterpreted from a single multiple-choice visual-correspondence experiment with custom hard distractors and one model family. The evidence supports a scaling observation, not a robust emergent phenomenon.

Proprietary-model comparison is not clearly fair: the paper adds extra prompts and GPT-4 post-processing for baselines, and it is unclear whether the same post-processing and prompt engineering are applied symmetrically. Format sensitivity may explain much of the reported gap.

Quantitative spatial accuracy remains low for important tasks (e.g., camera translation vector 18.0%, object movement vector 12.9%), which undercuts claims of robust multi-frame spatial understanding. The 20% L2-norm and 5%-image-width thresholds are lenient and may overstate performance.

Dynamic data generation may conflate camera-induced apparent motion with real object motion. The paper does not convincingly specify the coordinate frame and ground-truth construction for object-movement QA when both camera and object move, creating ambiguity in a central task.

The novelty is incremental relative to prior spatial MLLM work: the architecture is unchanged, and the main new resource is a template-generated dataset/benchmark. The paper does not isolate how much of the gain comes from data scale, task format, LoRA training, or model capacity.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the project page is not accessible in the submission, the full 27M QA dataset and generation code are not clearly released, and the listings are simplified rather than end-to-end reproducible, with stochastic GPT-4o template generation.

The '36% gain' phrasing in the main text is misleading: Table 2 shows +35.68 percentage points over the base model, not a 36% relative improvement. This is a presentation issue, but it affects interpretation of the headline result.

Generalization evidence is thin: BLINK gains occur on selected splits, with no improvement on the Spatial Reasoning split, and VQA results are mostly slightly worse than InternVL-8B (VizWiz, MathVista, MMStar, CCBench). Thus the claim of broad general-purpose spatial ability is not fully supported.

strengths: The paper introduces MultiSPA, the first large-scale dataset for multi-frame spatial understanding with over 27M QA samples and a comprehensive benchmark, addressing a real gap in MLLM spatial reasoning beyond single images.

The data generation pipeline is technically well-designed, leveraging existing 3D/4D datasets (ScanNet, ADT, PStudio, TAPVid3D) with point cloud projection, camera pose, and visible-point checks to produce diverse spatial QA tasks and output formats.

Extensive experiments are provided: fine-tuned 8B InternVL2 with LoRA, comparisons against proprietary models, held-out BLINK evaluation, standard VQA benchmarks, scaling trends, multi-task synergy, and robot demonstration.

The model achieves large improvements over open-source baselines and competitive or superior results compared with proprietary models on the MultiSPA benchmark, supporting the usefulness of the generated data.

Multi-task training benefits are empirically studied, with camera-movement and object-movement tasks improving when trained with additional task data, suggesting positive transfer across spatial tasks.
Generalization results are encouraging: zero-shot BLINK performance and standard VQA evaluations indicate that fine-tuning on MultiSPA does not catastrophically forget general capabilities.
The paper includes useful appendices with algorithm listings, data templates, source dataset details, and limitations, improving reproducibility relative to typical dataset papers.
The robotics demonstration suggests practical utility as a multi-frame reward annotator, pointing to downstream applications beyond benchmark accuracy.
weaknesses: The benchmark is largely in-domain: most benchmark samples come from the same source datasets used for training, and although disjoint scenes are claimed, a fully held-out multi-frame benchmark is not provided, limiting conclusions about generalization.
The 'multi-frame' contribution is often reduced to two-frame pairs; object size perception is restricted to only two images in the appendix, which weakens the claim of reasoning over multiple frames.

Several quantitative tasks remain far from solved, and the evaluation metrics are not fully specified or are lenient, e.g., vector predictions are considered correct within a 20% relative error, and object size/depth accuracy criteria lack detail.

Comparisons with proprietary models may be one-sided: baselines are evaluated zero-shot with prompts and GPT-4 post-processing, whereas the proposed model is fine-tuned on the target data distribution.

The data generation relies on automated templates and GPT-4o plus noisy 3D annotations; there is no human quality assessment, and ambiguous or unnatural QA pairs could inflate apparent benchmark performance.

The 'emergent' spatial reasoning claim is supported by only one hard multiple-choice split and one model family (InternVL2); capacity/encoder differences could explain the observed behavior, so the emergence conclusion is preliminary.

Only 3M of the 27M generated QA samples are used for training in the main experiments due to compute limits, meaning the claimed dataset scale is not fully exploited and the true scaling potential is unclear.
The paper lacks an explicit code/data release statement, and reproducibility is further constrained by the use of GPT-4o-generated templates and unspecified train/benchmark split details.

Comparisons with expert models show the method does not surpass specialized systems such as VGGT, DepthAnything, or LoFTR; the 'matching' claim is modest and may not justify strong multi-frame spatial understanding conclusions.

Dynamic data from point tracking and camera extrinsics may produce noisy ground truth, especially for small motions, and the paper does not analyze label noise or question ambiguity in these settings.

strengths: The paper presents a substantial data-engineering contribution: a GPU/point-cloud-based pipeline that produces pixel-aligned spatial QA pairs with diverse referencing (dots, coordinates, semantics) and output formats (qualitative, scalar, MCQ, coordinate/vector) from existing 3D/4D annotated datasets (ScanNet, ADT, PSStudio, TAPVid3D). The pipeline is described with concrete formulas and algorithm listings, which aids reproducibility.

The external transfer results are genuinely informative in places. Zero-shot transfer to BLINK (Table 3, 84.3 avg vs 57.9 for InternVL-8B, beating GPT-4o and Gemini-2.0) is a nontrivial and interesting signal that multi-frame spatial training helps outside the authors' own benchmark, especially on visual correspondence and multi-view splits.

The multi-task synergy studies (Tables 5, 12, 13) provide concrete, quantitative evidence that training on multiple spatial tasks improves individual tasks beyond single-task training — a useful practical finding.

The demonstrations (Fig. 5, reward annotator) are compelling as motivating applications, and the forgetting-curve evidence (Fig. 6, Table 4/11) is a reasonable attempt to show the model is not simply overfit to spatial tasks.
The paper is generally well-written and clear in its formulation, with a useful dataset comparison (Table 1) and reasonable implementation details (LoRA rank, learning rate, batch size, hardware).
weaknesses: The headline result (Table 2: +35.68 average gain, surpassing proprietary models) is on the authors' own benchmark using a model they fine-tuned on data generated from the same pipeline. Baselines (Claude-3.5, Gemini-2.0, GPT-4o, InternVL) are used zero-shot, so the comparison conflates spatial ability with instruction-following/answer-format adaptation. The claim that Multi-SpatialMLLM 'matches or exceeds' proprietary systems is not adequately substantiated by a same-conditions comparison.

The most relevant concurrent multi-frame spatial works are absent from the empirical comparison. Spatial-MLLM, VLM-3R, SAT, and multi-frame/spatial benchmarks such as VSI-Bench and MVBench are cited but not evaluated against (Table 1 even excludes SAT), so the novelty and relative strength of 'multi-frame' spatial understanding over prior art is unclear.

The 'multi-frame' framing is oversold relative to what is actually done. Depth perception and depth comparison are single-image tasks; object-size perception is limited to two images (per the BFS section, because the search 'becomes expensive when considering sets of three or more images'); and training is entirely on image pairs. Generalization to more frames is relegated to the appendix (Table 14), so 'multi-frame' is effectively pairwise throughout the main paper.

The 'emergence of spatial understanding' claim (Sec. 4.3, Table 6) is weakly supported. It rests on a single multiple-choice visual-correspondence task, and the compared configurations are confounded (different model families and encoder sizes, e.g. 8B/300M vs 26B/6B), so attributing the gap to model scale alone is not justified by the evidence presented.

Much of the 27M-sample dataset is generated by combining a handful of existing datasets with GPT-4o-produced templates and programmatic GT extraction. This means the 'scale' is largely templating (≈25 QA per image from ~1.1M images) rather than newly collected annotations, and it is unclear how much of the training signal is genuine spatial reasoning versus template/format following. No diversity analysis of the QA distribution or redundancy statistics are provided.

The evaluation metric thresholds are self-defined and relatively permissive (2% relative error for vectors, 5% image width for coordinates), and there is no reported confidence interval or inter-annotator/parsing reliability analysis. Given that the benchmark and data are from the same source, a potential leakage/familiarity concern remains even though scene-level splits are claimed to be disjoint.

Generalization comparisons with expert models are not conclusive: Table 9 shows the model trailing VGGT (86 vs 82) and Depth-Anything (86 vs 76) on visually complex tasks, so attributing the result to 'matching' specialized systems is optimistic given the different evaluation conditions (fully fine-tuned 26B variant used for camera vector, 8B for others).

Reproducibility is incomplete for practical use: no data/code/model release link is provided in the paper, and given the reliance on external datasets (ScanNet, ADT, PSStudio, TAPVid3D) with varying licensing, the actual release of the 27M-sample dataset and benchmark remains unclear.

The reward-annotator demonstration is anecdotal. Figure 5 shows one static-cube scenario and a rough distance trend; no quantitative evaluation of the annotation quality relative to ground truth is provided.
